newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe stresses Europe, unity for French election.
newsitem.headline: Juppe stresses Europe, unity for French election.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe rallied his forces on Tuesday for a snap parliamentary election, pledging more of the same economic medicine and stressing his commitment to further European integration.

Addressing parliamentarians and senior members of his often fractious centre-right coalition at a conference centre in western Paris, Juppe promised an aggressive campaign that he said would win the election to lead a modernised France into the next century.
On Monday, in the most daring gamble since taking office, President Jacques Chirac dissolved the National Assembly and brought forward the election by 10 months to May 25 and June 1.

He argued that France needed a government with a renewed legitimacy to prepare for a single European currency and reform the state, cutting public spending and taxes. The Socialist-led opposition accused Chirac of preparing a new bout of austerity.
France's European partners see Chirac's decision as a bold roll of the dice that could make or break economic and monetary union (EMU).

Juppe said his party would build a modern, slimmed down state, free companies from over-regulation, cut spending and taxes and continue to build a "grand Europe" with a single currency while defending France's interests.
"France has nothing to fear but everything to gain from the euro, everything to gain from the Union, everything to gain from Europe," he said. "Let us be the motor of this great adventure."
"National interest dictates that we must win because France cannot allow itself another Socialist fiasco," he said to cheers and applause.
But he denied he planned a sharp turn to the right with more free market policies and less social protection, as opposition Socialists and trade unions have charged.
The political scene plunged into the campaign on Tuesday and the government postponed its biggest privatisation project, the sale of a minority stake in France Telecom SA.

The Socialists have threatened to renationalise the telecommunications giant, in which a 30 percent stake worth an estimated 30 to 50 billion francs ($5.2 billion to $8.7 billion) was due to have been floated next month.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said the sale would be put off by four weeks, arguing it required a large public relations campaign difficult to hold during an election.
Analysts said the decision was wise since it removed the political uncertainty weighing on the sell-off.

Financial markets, still jittery from uncertainty generated by the early poll, began a comeback. The franc and fixed income markets were stronger on the view the conservatives were likely to keep a majority, dealers said.
The stock market opened higher but faded to close down 0.32 percent, its third consecutive drop.
Former Socialist prime minister Laurent Fabius said the snap election decision could yet backfire on Chirac.

"Will the French say 'bravo' to the rise in unemployment, 'great' to the rise in taxes, 'well done' for the increase in poverty? I doubt it," the Socialist parliamentary floor leader told Europe 1 radio.
He said the left had a 50-50 chance of victory. Opinion polls taken before Chirac's announcement suggested the opposition's chances were more remote.
The centre-right coalition held a massive 464 seats in the outgoing 577-member chamber, giving it a formidable advantage of incumbency despite Chirac's and Juppe's deep unpopularity.
Jean-Francois Mancel, secretary general of Chirac's RPR party, denounced as "brazen lies" opposition charges that the government planned a new bout of austerity after the campaign.
But a senior government official told Reuters that further austerity would be required in the autumn to meet the deficit limits required to qualify for a single European currency.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin accused Chirac of veering towards a harsher brand of capitalism. Far-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen accused the president of an "electoral hold-up, a shameful swindle".
The main issue for French voters is unemployment -- which has risen to 12.8 percent of the workforce from 11.7 percent when Chirac took office two years ago promising a war for jobs.
